idiom_name: deadpool managed::Pool<Manager> with Drop-based return (r2d2 for blocking pools)
implementation_notes: In Rust the pool is a crate and the lease is a guard: deadpool's managed Pool needs a Manager whose create()/recycle() hooks build and validate instances, pool.get().await yields an Object that returns itself to the pool when it is dropped, and bounds/fairness come from a Semaphore (timeouts require enabling a runtime feature). deadpool::unmanaged::Pool covers instances you construct yourself, and r2d2 is the blocking counterpart for sync code. The ownership system enforces the pattern's return path - there is no release() call to forget - but it also means recycle errors surface on the next get() rather than at drop time, because Drop cannot be async.
code_sketch:
let pool = managed::Pool::builder(mgr).build().unwrap();   // max_size(...) caps it
let mut conn = pool.get().await.unwrap();   // checked out
conn.exec(sql).await?;                      // dropped at scope end -> recycled
pitfalls: Holding an Object across a long await starves the pool exactly like a forgotten release elsewhere; keep the guard scoped to the operation that needs it.
Because return happens in Drop, a pool full of dead connections looks healthy until the next checkout discovers the recycle failure - validate on get/recycle, not only on create.
Pooled types must be Send + 'static and manager hooks must not block: a std::sync::Mutex held across an await, or a blocking connect() inside create(), stalls the executor.
